title: Fatigue, jaundice and a leg rash in a 63-year-old painter
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 63-year-old man who has had fatigue for several months. He is jaundiced and has a recurrent purpuric rash on his legs. The candidate then interprets his liver and blood tests and his hepatitis serology, recognises chronic hepatitis C with cirrhosis and probable cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, and plans investigation, referral, treatment and safety netting in general practice.
focus: Fatigue history that uncovers a blood-borne virus risk: recognising chronic hepatitis C with cirrhosis and extrahepatic vasculitis, and interpreting liver tests and hepatitis serology
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a suburban general practice. Minh Nguyen, a 63-year-old painter, has come in because he has been feeling tired for the last few months. When he walks in, you notice that his skin and the whites of his eyes look yellow, and that he has a rash on his lower legs. Your GP supervisor will see him after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Minh and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Minh's blood test results and hepatitis serology. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Minh Nguyen, a 63-year-old self-employed house painter. You are polite, a bit stoic and you hate to "make a fuss". You have avoided doctors most of your life. You are embarrassed about your past drug use: you are open about it only if you are asked directly and without judgement. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I've just been really tired for the last few months, doctor. Probably just getting old."

The tiredness (give only when asked):

  • You cannot remember the last time you felt completely well. It has crept up gradually over the last few months, and you put it down to "getting old".
  • It is hard to describe. It is not sleepiness and you are not down or low. Sometimes your head feels foggy and you find it hard to concentrate at work.
  • Rest does not help, and it is not linked to how much you do.
  • It is now affecting your work: you are slower and finding the physical work harder.

The rash:

  • Only on your lower legs. You noticed it in the shower a week ago.
  • It is bumpy, but not itchy or painful. Nothing seems to bring it on.
  • You have had about five rashes like this over the past year. Each one went away by itself within a week.

Other symptoms (give the positives when asked):

  • Possibly a little weight loss over the last 12 months without trying ("my work pants are a bit loose").
  • Your tummy feels slightly fuller and a bit uncomfortable.
  • A workmate said last week that your skin and eyes look yellow.
  • Your poo may be a bit paler than usual.

Negatives (if asked): no fevers or night sweats. No recent travel or sick contacts. Appetite is normal. No easy bruising or bleeding, no vomiting blood or black stools. No itch. No trouble swallowing, no abdominal pain as such, no vomiting. No chest pain, breathlessness, cough, waking breathless at night, needing extra pillows, or ankle swelling. No lumps in your neck, armpits or groin. No joint pains, and no jaw pain when chewing. No numbness, tingling or burning in your feet or hands. Your mood is fine, you still enjoy things, and your sleep has not changed.

Past medical history: you have avoided doctors, so you have no known conditions. No operations, no blood transfusions, no transplants. No tattoos (if asked).

Medicines: an anti-inflammatory (ibuprofen) now and then for aches and pains from work, and paracetamol rarely. No regular medicines. Vaccinations: you have had tetanus-whooping cough (dTpa) boosters. You think the methadone clinic gave you a course of three injections, possibly hepatitis B, but you are not sure. You are not sure about any others, and you have no childhood records.

Allergies: none.

Family history: you were born in Vietnam and came to Australia with your mother when you were 12. You do not know your father's medical history. Your mother died at 83 after a stroke. Your sister, 51, has high blood pressure.

Social history:

  • Smoking: since your teens. About 10 a day for 20 years, now about 5 a day.
  • Alcohol: three cans of beer in a session, once or twice a week.
  • Drugs (only if asked directly): in your early 20s you used cannabis and injected heroin for about five years. You can't be sure you never shared equipment. You completed a methadone program and have not used any drugs for about 30 years. You have never been tested for hepatitis or HIV.
  • Sexual history (if asked): last sexually active 4 years ago, with women only, and used condoms only some of the time.
  • Work: self-employed house painter, which is physically demanding.
  • Diet: worse since you have been tired; more takeaway.
  • Home: you live alone. You are divorced and your adult son lives interstate. You have a strong network of friends.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: it is just getting older.
  • Concern (say this when asked how it affects you, or about work): "I can't keep up at work. I'm worried I'll be forced to retire, and I can't afford that."
  • Expectation: you did not want to make a fuss, but your workmate told you to get checked. You expect a blood test.

Question to raise near the end of the history: "Is this just my age, do you reckon?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General: lean build, clothes slightly loose, comfortable at rest, alert and orientated. Obviously jaundiced. Weight 66 kg, height 170 cm, BMI 23 kg/m².
  • Observations: BP 126/76 mmHg, HR 84/min regular, RR 14/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C. Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L.
  • Hands: palmar erythema on both hands. No clubbing, leuconychia or Dupuytren's contracture. No asterixis (flap).
  • Face and neck: yellow sclerae. No parotid enlargement. JVP not raised.
  • Chest: three spider naevi on the upper chest. No gynaecomastia. No scratch marks. Heart sounds dual with no murmurs; chest clear.
  • Abdomen: mildly distended. No caput medusae. Soft, with mild discomfort in the right upper quadrant on deep palpation. Liver edge not palpable. Spleen tip palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin on deep inspiration, non-tender. No shifting dullness. No masses. Rectal examination not performed in this station.
  • Lymph nodes: no cervical, supraclavicular, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
  • Legs: raised (palpable) purple spots, 2 to 4 mm, on both shins and the tops of both feet, up to mid-calf. They do not blanch under a glass. No ulcers or necrosis. No ankle oedema.
  • Joints: no swelling or tenderness.
  • Urine dipstick (if asked): bilirubin positive; blood and protein negative.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Minh's identity, explains the purpose of the consultation and gains consent for the examination.
Asks about drug use and sexual history in a normalising, non-judgemental way, uses plain language, and acknowledges his reluctance to "make a fuss" and his worry about being forced to retire.
History
Characterises the fatigue:

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual over months, cannot remember last feeling well, blamed on getting old.
Character: not sleepiness or low mood; brain fog and poor concentration; not helped by rest and unrelated to activity.
Impact: now affecting his physically demanding work.

check.x: Characterises the rash:

kids.x: Site and onset: lower legs only, noticed a week ago in the shower.
Symptoms: not itchy or painful; nothing provokes it.
Recurrence: about five similar rashes over the past year, each resolving within a week.

check.x: Asks hepatobiliary and gastrointestinal questions: yellow skin and eyes (noticed by a workmate), stool colour (maybe paler), abdominal fullness or discomfort (slightly fuller), itch, bruising or bleeding, vomiting blood or black stools, swallowing [itch, bleeding and swallowing problems absent].
Screens for constitutional symptoms and malignancy: weight loss (possibly a little over 12 months), fevers, night sweats, appetite, lumps or swollen glands [only the weight loss present].

Screens other systems for causes of fatigue: cardiac (chest pain, orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling), respiratory (breathlessness, cough), rheumatological (joint pain, jaw claudication), neurological (numbness, tingling), mood (anhedonia, sleep change), and travel or sick contacts [all negative].
check.d: Award for at least two systems beyond hepatobiliary and GI.

check.x: Takes a blood-borne virus risk history: injected heroin for about five years in his early 20s, possibly shared equipment, completed methadone, no drug use for about 30 years, never tested for hepatitis or HIV; asks about transfusions and tattoos (none).

Takes the past medical, medication, allergy and immunisation history: no known conditions (avoids doctors), occasional NSAIDs and rare paracetamol, no allergies, dTpa boosters, possibly a hepatitis B course at the methadone clinic, other vaccines uncertain.
Quantifies alcohol (three cans a session, once or twice a week) and smoking (since his teens, 10 a day for about 20 years, now 5 a day).

Takes the family and social history: born in Vietnam and came to Australia at 12; father's history unknown, mother died of a stroke at 83, sister has hypertension; self-employed painter, lives alone, divorced, son interstate, good friends; sexual history (last partner 4 years ago, inconsistent condom use).
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is his age, worried about being forced to retire, came only because his workmate urged him.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs, including weight or BMI [jaundiced, lean, observations normal, BMI 23].

Looks for peripheral signs of chronic liver disease: hands (palmar erythema, clubbing, leuconychia, Dupuytren's), sclerae, spider naevi, gynaecomastia and scratch marks [palmar erythema, scleral icterus, three spider naevi].

Examines the abdomen: inspects for distension and caput medusae, palpates for the liver and spleen, percusses for ascites (shifting dullness) [mild distension, RUQ discomfort, liver not palpable, spleen tip palpable, no shifting dullness].
Examines the rash: distribution, whether it is raised, and tests for blanching (glass test), and looks for ulceration [palpable non-blanching purpura on both shins and feet, no ulcers].
Examines the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal lymph nodes [none palpable].
Assesses for complications and other causes: asterixis and orientation (encephalopathy), ankle oedema, JVP and heart sounds (congestive cause) [all normal].
check.d: Credit, but do not require: asks for a urine dipstick for blood and protein (glomerulonephritis) [bilirubin positive, no blood or protein].

check.x: Interpretation

Full blood count: Hb 135 with normal indices, so no anaemia to explain the fatigue; normal white cells and differential; platelets low at 120, suggesting portal hypertension with splenic sequestration.
Bilirubin 60 with a raised conjugated fraction (30) and a normal haptoglobin: hepatic (hepatobiliary) jaundice, not haemolysis.

Liver enzymes: ALT 80 and AST 50 mildly raised with a normal ALP and mildly raised GGT: a mild hepatocellular pattern suggesting a chronic process; AST:ALT below 1 is against alcohol as the main cause.
Synthetic function: albumin 29 and INR 1.4 show impaired liver synthetic function; with the low platelets and jaundice this suggests cirrhosis.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: APRI about 1.2 (above 1, so cirrhosis possible); Child-Pugh B (score 8).

check.x: Hepatitis A and B: anti-HBs positive with HBsAg and anti-HBc negative means immune from vaccination, not past or current infection; anti-HAV detected means immune to hepatitis A (no vaccine needed).
Hepatitis C: anti-HCV positive with HCV RNA detected means current (chronic) hepatitis C infection, and states that antibody alone would not distinguish current from cleared infection.

Gives the most likely diagnosis as cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C, with the recurrent palpable purpura probably cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, linked to his past injecting drug use, and says imaging is needed to confirm cirrhosis.

Names differentials with a feature for or against from this case: other or additional causes of cirrhosis (alcohol, MASLD, haemochromatosis, congestive), hepatocellular carcinoma or liver metastases, lymphoma or leukaemia, and one other group (vasculitis, depression, endocrine).
check.d: Full marks needs hepatobiliary and malignancy causes plus one other group.

check.x: Management

Explains the diagnosis to Minh in plain language: a virus in the liver, probably from injecting many years ago, which has scarred the liver; it is curable with tablets; responds to his questions about blame and work without judgement.
Arranges further investigations:

kids.x: Urgent liver ultrasound with Doppler and alpha-fetoprotein, to confirm cirrhosis and look for hepatocellular carcinoma, ascites and portal vein patency.
Assesses fibrosis with transient elastography (FibroScan), or calculates APRI.
Further tests: HIV serology, and tests for cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis (cryoglobulins, C4/rheumatoid factor or urine ACR).

check.x: Refers urgently to hepatology (gastroenterology) because he has features of decompensated cirrhosis (jaundice, low albumin, raised INR), for specialist-led antiviral treatment, gastroscopy to screen for varices and assessment for transplant if needed.

Outlines antiviral treatment: specialist-led direct-acting antiviral tablets (PBS-listed) for about 12 weeks, curing about 9 in 10; cure is confirmed by an undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment ends.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: names sofosbuvir/velpatasvir with ribavirin for 12 weeks (24 weeks without ribavirin); states that protease inhibitor regimens (e.g. glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) are contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis; checks drug interactions.

check.x: Protects the liver: stops NSAIDs (paracetamol is the preferred analgesic, at a reduced maximum of 2 g a day in decompensated cirrhosis), advises no alcohol, checks hepatitis A immunity (immune, no vaccine needed), and offers smoking cessation support and nutrition advice.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: influenza and pneumococcal vaccination; dietitian referral.

check.x: Safety netting
Tells him to call 000 or go to ED for vomiting blood or black, tarry stools, new confusion or drowsiness, or fever with abdominal pain or a rapidly swelling abdomen.
Tells him to see the GP promptly for a spreading or ulcerating rash, blood in or frothy urine, new leg swelling, worsening yellowing or itch, or easy bruising.

Arranges follow-up: GP review within a week with the ultrasound and further results, confirming the hepatology appointment; lifelong 6-monthly liver ultrasound for liver cancer surveillance, even after cure.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: written information; National Hepatitis Infoline 1800 437 222 or Hepatitis Australia.

check.x: Public health: hepatitis C is notifiable; no sharing of razors, toothbrushes or injecting equipment, cover cuts, no blood donation.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: offers testing to anyone who may have been exposed.

part2.lead: Your supervisor ordered blood tests at the end of the consultation. Minh is back a week later for his results. Here are his blood tests and his hepatitis serology.
part2.patient:
Minh stays silent during the handover and the differentials. When the candidate explains the diagnosis and plan to him (Questions 3 and 4), ask:

  • "Hepatitis C? Is that from the drugs? That was 30 years ago. I've been clean ever since." Be embarrassed, and relieved if the candidate is not judgemental.
  • "Can it be fixed?" Be relieved to hear it is usually cured with tablets.
  • "Will I have to stop working?" A good answer: treatment is tablets, the fatigue often improves once the virus is cleared, and a medical certificate can be given if he needs time off. Be reassured if you hear this.

handover.label: Blood tests (full blood count, liver function, coagulation, kidney function, TSH, iron studies)
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 135 with normal indices; WCC and differential normal; platelets low at 120. Total bilirubin 60 with conjugated 30, about half conjugated; haptoglobin normal. ALT 80, AST 50, GGT 80 mildly raised; ALP normal. Albumin low at 29; INR raised at 1.4. Renal function, TSH and iron studies normal.
  • For Minh: no anaemia to explain the fatigue. The jaundice is hepatic, not haemolytic (normal haptoglobin, normal Hb). A mild hepatocellular pattern with normal ALP suggests chronic liver disease rather than obstruction; AST:ALT below 1 is against alcohol as the main driver. Low albumin, high INR and high bilirubin show impaired synthetic function, and low platelets with a palpable spleen suggest portal hypertension: together, cirrhosis. APRI = (50/35) / 120 x 100 = about 1.2, above 1. Child-Pugh B (score 8): decompensated.
  • What it changes: needs urgent ultrasound with AFP, elastography, and urgent hepatology referral; stop NSAIDs.

handover.label: Hepatitis serology
handover.result: Collected at 08:30 with the blood tests above. Lab comment: Hepatitis C is a notifiable condition.
handover.model:
• Read: hepatitis A total antibody detected. HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBe and anti-HBc (IgM and total) not detected; anti-HBs 85 mIU/mL. Anti-HCV detected and HCV RNA detected at 1.8 x 10^6 IU/mL.
  • For Minh: hepatitis B: immune from vaccination (surface antibody only, no core antibody), so no past or current infection despite being born in Vietnam. Hepatitis A: immune, as expected for someone who grew up in Vietnam. Hepatitis C: antibody shows exposure, and detectable RNA shows current infection. With 35 to 40 years since he first injected (no drug use for about 30 years) and these blood results, this is chronic hepatitis C, the likely cause of his cirrhosis. The recurrent palpable purpura fits mixed cryoglobulinaemia, an extrahepatic manifestation.
  • What it changes: he needs direct-acting antiviral treatment (specialist-led because of decompensation), HIV testing, notification, and advice on preventing transmission; no hepatitis A or B vaccine is needed.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Minh Nguyen, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Minh now, here in general practice.
Before Minh goes home today, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; Minh Nguyen, 63.
  • Situation: months of fatigue, jaundice and recurrent palpable purpura; bloods show chronic hepatitis C with probable cirrhosis.
  • Background: injected heroin in his 20s, never tested; born in Vietnam; occasional NSAIDs; modest alcohol; smoker. Exam: jaundice, palmar erythema, spider naevi, spleen tip, purpura on both legs.
  • Assessment: Hb normal; platelets 120. Bilirubin 60, half conjugated, haptoglobin normal: hepatic, not haemolysis. ALT 80, AST 50, ALP normal: chronic hepatocellular. Albumin 29, INR 1.4: impaired synthesis, suggesting cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B). Anti-HCV and RNA positive: current HCV. HBV vaccinated; HAV immune.
  • Recommendation: urgent ultrasound with AFP, elastography, urgent hepatology referral; stop NSAIDs.

Most likely: cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C, with cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis. For: past injecting, never tested; HCV RNA positive; jaundice, low albumin, high INR, low platelets, splenomegaly, stigmata; recurrent palpable purpura.

  • Other or added causes of cirrhosis (alcohol, MASLD, haemochromatosis, congestive): drinks 4 to 8 a week, but AST:ALT below 1; normal BMI; JVP not raised; normal transferrin saturation and ferritin argue against haemochromatosis.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma or metastases: weight loss, smoker, cirrhosis; needs ultrasound and AFP.
  • Lymphoma or leukaemia (HCV-associated): weight loss, fatigue; but no nodes, sweats or fevers and a normal differential.
  • Depression or hypothyroidism: fatigue and brain fog; but no low mood or anhedonia, normal TSH excludes hypothyroidism, and neither explains the jaundice or purpura.

1. Explain without judgement: hepatitis C has scarred the liver; it is curable with tablets.
  2. Investigate: urgent liver ultrasound with Doppler and AFP; FibroScan (APRI about 1.2); HIV serology, and tests for cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis (cryoglobulins, C4/RF or urine ACR).
  3. Refer urgently to hepatology: jaundice, albumin 29 and INR 1.4 mean decompensation (Child-Pugh B), so treatment is specialist-led; gastroscopy for varices; transplant assessment if needed.
  4. Treat (specialist-led): DAA tablets about 12 weeks, cure about 9 in 10, HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment (credit: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir + ribavirin; no protease inhibitors in decompensation).
  5. Protect the liver: stop NSAIDs; paracetamol is the preferred analgesic, at a reduced maximum of 2 g a day in decompensated cirrhosis; no alcohol; hepatitis A immune, no vaccine needed; quit smoking; nutrition.

Call 000 or go to ED:

  • vomiting blood, or black, tarry stools
  • confusion, drowsiness or behaving strangely
  • fever with tummy pain, or a fast-swelling tummy

See the GP promptly: rash spreading or ulcerating, blood in or frothy urine, leg swelling, worse yellowing or itch, easy bruising.

Prevent spread: notifiable; don't share razors, toothbrushes or injecting gear; cover cuts; don't donate blood.

Follow-up:

  • GP review within a week with the ultrasound and further results; confirm the hepatology appointment
  • after cure, 6-monthly liver ultrasound for life for liver cancer; reinfection is possible
  • credit, not required: written information; National Hepatitis Infoline 1800 437 222 or Hepatitis Australia

ddx.dx: Cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C, with cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis
ddx.for: Past injecting drug use and never tested, HCV antibody and RNA positive, jaundice with low albumin, raised INR, low platelets, splenomegaly and spider naevi, and recurrent palpable purpura on the legs.

ddx.dx: Cirrhosis from another or additional cause (alcohol, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, haemochromatosis, congestive hepatopathy)
ddx.for: He drinks about four standard drinks a session once or twice a week, and cirrhosis is present.
ddx.against: AST:ALT is below 1, his BMI is 23, the JVP is not raised and he has no breathlessness or oedema, HCV RNA is detected, and normal transferrin saturation and ferritin argue against haemochromatosis.

ddx.for: Born in Vietnam, where hepatitis B is common, with unknown vaccination history.
ddx.against: HBsAg and core antibody are negative and surface antibody is positive, so he is immune from vaccination.

ddx.for: Unintentional weight loss, jaundice, a smoking history and probable cirrhosis from hepatitis C.
ddx.against: No mass on examination, but this cannot be excluded without an ultrasound and AFP.

ddx.dx: Lymphoma or leukaemia (including hepatitis C-associated B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma)
ddx.for: Fatigue, weight loss, purpura and a palpable spleen, with chronic hepatitis C.
ddx.against: No fevers, sweats or lymphadenopathy, and a normal white cell count, differential and haemoglobin.

ddx.dx: Depression or an endocrine cause of fatigue such as hypothyroidism
ddx.for: Fatigue, brain fog and poor concentration in a man who lives alone.
ddx.against: No low mood, anhedonia or sleep change, normal TSH excludes hypothyroidism, and neither explains the jaundice, purpura or abnormal liver tests.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Minh talks about his injecting drug use only when asked directly about drugs. He raises his worry about retiring when asked how the fatigue affects him or about work.

In Part 2 hand over both results together and ask the four questions in order. Minh stays silent for Questions 1 and 2, and puts his questions while the candidate explains to him in Questions 3 and 4. Credit, but do not require: APRI, the Child-Pugh score, and naming sofosbuvir/velpatasvir.

A high-performing candidate characterises the fatigue and the recurrent rash, screens for malignancy, and finds the injecting drug history without judgement. They examine for stigmata of chronic liver disease, splenomegaly and ascites, and test the rash for blanching. In Part 2 they separate hepatic jaundice from haemolysis, read impaired synthetic function as cirrhosis, read the hepatitis B pattern as vaccination and the HCV RNA as current infection, and link the purpura to cryoglobulinaemia. They arrange an urgent ultrasound with AFP, refer urgently to hepatology because of decompensation, stop NSAIDs, and give specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic fatigue history and misses the drug history or the recurrent rash. They call the anti-HBs "hepatitis B infection", treat antibody alone as proof of current infection, or miss the low albumin and INR. They plan GP treatment without recognising decompensation, forget the NSAIDs, or give vague safety netting.
explain:
The clue is in the social history

Fatigue is a vague presentation, and the key to it often sits in the social or family history. Here it is injecting drug use, birth overseas and an unknown immunisation history. Minh injected heroin for five years in his 20s, was never tested for blood-borne viruses, and has avoided doctors since. Fatigue, abdominal fullness, weight loss, pale stools and jaundice point to the liver. The recurrent, self-limiting palpable purpura on his legs is a small-vessel vasculitis, and with hepatitis C the likely cause is mixed cryoglobulinaemia.

Hepatitis C in Australia

Risk factors are injecting drug use (the main one), blood transfusion before 1990, perinatal transmission and unsafe tattooing or body piercing. About 10 to 30% of people with untreated chronic infection develop cirrhosis over 20 years. Hepatitis C cirrhosis has been one of the leading causes of liver transplantation and liver cancer in Australia. Extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis C include mixed cryoglobulinaemia (palpable purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy), membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, sicca syndrome, thyroiditis and B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. In contrast, hepatitis B is classically linked to polyarteritis nodosa.

Interpreting the results

  • No anaemia: Hb is normal, so anaemia does not explain the fatigue.
  • Jaundice: the conjugated fraction is raised and haptoglobin is normal, so this is hepatic (hepatobiliary) jaundice, not haemolysis. A normal ALP makes obstruction less likely, but ultrasound is still needed.
  • Enzymes: a mild rise in ALT and AST with a normal ALP is a hepatocellular pattern. Mild rises like this are typical of chronic viral hepatitis. An AST:ALT ratio above 2 would point more to alcohol. Note that in established cirrhosis of any cause the ratio often rises above 1, so it is a soft pointer only.
  • Synthetic function and portal hypertension: low albumin, a raised INR (not on anticoagulants) and raised bilirubin mean the liver is failing to synthesise. Low platelets with a palpable spleen suggest portal hypertension. Together these suggest cirrhosis. APRI = (AST / upper limit of normal) / platelets x 100 = (50/35) / 120 x 100, about 1.2. An APRI below 1 makes cirrhosis unlikely; at 1 or above, cirrhosis needs to be assessed with elastography. His Child-Pugh score is about 8: bilirubin above 50 (3), albumin 28 to 35 (2), INR below 1.7 (1), no ascites (1), no encephalopathy (1). That is class B, so he has decompensated disease.
  • Other tests: normal renal function despite his NSAID use; a normal TSH excludes hypothyroidism; normal ferritin and transferrin saturation argue against haemochromatosis.
  • Hepatitis B: surface antibody alone, with no core antibody, means immunity from vaccination. Core antibody with surface antibody would mean past infection; HBsAg would mean current infection.
  • Hepatitis A: total antibody detected, so he is immune (most likely from childhood infection in Vietnam) and no vaccine is needed. People with chronic liver disease who are not immune should be vaccinated.
  • Hepatitis C: antibody shows exposure but stays positive after spontaneous clearance or cure. A detectable HCV RNA confirms current infection; the quantified viral load is a baseline for the specialist.

Differentials

Consider other or additional causes of cirrhosis (alcohol, MASLD, haemochromatosis, congestive hepatopathy). Malignancy must be considered: hepatocellular carcinoma in a cirrhotic liver, liver metastases (he smokes and has lost weight), and lymphoma or leukaemia, which hepatitis C makes more likely. Other causes of purpura include primary vasculitides. Other causes of fatigue include depression and endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism.

Management

  • Confirm and stage: liver ultrasound with Doppler (cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, ascites, portal vein) and AFP; transient elastography; HIV serology; urinalysis with ACR (cryoglobulinaemic glomerulonephritis), repeating renal function if NSAIDs continue; cryoglobulins, C4 and rheumatoid factor (the cryoglobulin sample must be collected and kept at 37 °C until it reaches the lab).
  • Refer: direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) are PBS-listed and can be prescribed in general practice. People with decompensated cirrhosis need specialist hepatology care. The specialist chooses the regimen, such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir with or without ribavirin. Protease inhibitor regimens (for example glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) are contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis. Specialists also arrange gastroscopy to screen for varices and assessment for transplantation.
  • Treatment and cure: in compensated disease, pangenotypic DAAs cure more than 95% of people over 8 to 12 weeks. In decompensated cirrhosis the regimen is sofosbuvir/velpatasvir with ribavirin for 12 weeks (or 24 weeks without ribavirin), and cure rates are lower, about 85-94%. Check for drug interactions before starting. Cure is confirmed by an undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment ends. Cure does not protect against reinfection. Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis often improves once the virus is cleared.
  • General measures: stop NSAIDs (in cirrhosis they risk kidney injury, bleeding and fluid retention). Paracetamol is the preferred analgesic, at a reduced maximum of 2 g a day in decompensated cirrhosis. Advise no alcohol, check hepatitis A and B immunity (he is immune to both, so no vaccine is needed), offer smoking cessation, and support his nutrition.
  • Surveillance: people with cirrhosis need 6-monthly liver ultrasound (with or without AFP) for hepatocellular carcinoma. This continues even after cure.
  • Public health: hepatitis C is notifiable. Advise him not to share razors, toothbrushes or injecting equipment, to cover cuts, and not to donate blood. Offer testing to anyone who may have been exposed.

Safety netting

Decompensated cirrhosis can deteriorate quickly. He needs 000 or ED for:

  • vomiting blood or black stools (variceal bleeding);
  • confusion or drowsiness (hepatic encephalopathy);
  • fever with abdominal pain or a rapidly swelling abdomen (ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis).

He should see the GP promptly if the rash spreads or ulcerates, or if he notices blood in his urine, frothy urine or swelling (glomerulonephritis). Address his work worries directly: treatment is tablets, and many people feel better once the virus is cleared.
points: Open-ended presentations such as fatigue often hide the key clue in the social history: ask every patient about injecting drug use, tattoos, transfusions and country of birth, without judgement.

Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a normal haptoglobin is hepatic, not haemolytic; low albumin, a raised INR and low platelets mean impaired synthetic function and portal hypertension, suggesting cirrhosis.
Anti-HBs alone means hepatitis B vaccination; anti-HCV shows exposure only, and a detectable HCV RNA confirms current infection.
Palpable purpura in hepatitis C suggests mixed cryoglobulinaemia; check cryoglobulins, complement C4 and the urine for glomerulonephritis.

Direct-acting antivirals cure more than 95% of people with hepatitis C and are PBS-listed for GP prescribing, but decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C) needs specialist-led treatment, usually sofosbuvir/velpatasvir with ribavirin for 12 weeks, with a lower cure rate.
In cirrhosis, stop NSAIDs, check hepatitis A and B immunity and vaccinate if not immune, avoid alcohol, and arrange 6-monthly ultrasound for hepatocellular carcinoma for life, even after cure.
